title: Manuel "Fess" Manetta and Edward "Kid" Ory Interview, 1958-08-26

blocks.x: We close enough?
Yeah, that's good enough.
Hold the test for the mic.
He'll pick up anything in the room, practically. Right there? Yeah, let's get back there. Pick up either you or Paz.
What are you going to say, Paz? Shoot it down.
No, that's all right, Paz. Just as if we were visiting. You don't have to worry.
How are you feeling, Paz? Oh, fine. How you been? Good.
How long since you saw one another? Not so long. How long has it been?
The night you would hang over for? About four years ago.
Four years?
Have you been well ever since? Oh, yeah.
Been well, but only the last past summer. Some high blood pressure. Now I'm feeling really good.
Well, you're looking all right, boy. Thank you. How long is it? You're looking fine. Same.
Do you remember the first time you all played together? About when it was, or where? Where's it?
Tom Anderson.
Tom Anderson. Was it Tom Anderson? Right across from 25th? Tom Anderson? Yeah.
Oh, we played several places. Yeah, well, but I mean that's the first time I recall. Oh, the first time? Yeah, about the first time.
Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah.
Oh, yeah.

Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. And what was the next? You remember? Can you recall, Chris? Depends on you a lot, Tom. Well, then you were playing a single there for a long time. Yeah. Sturerville. Yeah. Yeah. Sturerville. Yeah. Yeah. And I think the next time is when you came to Los Angeles in 1919, wasn't it? Well then you were playing a single there for a long time. Yeah.
Sturerville. Yeah.
I think the next time is when you came to Los Angeles in 1919, was it? 1919, yeah.
You all worked together at the Pete Lala's dance hall in Michigan?
Well, I worked at Pete Lala's. He worked there at Pete.
And you played there?
I never played for Pete Lala, no.
He had a better job than Pete Lala's job, this guy. What about that one?
You played violin there with Oliver. Was Kedori in the band then?
It was Ory and Oliver's jazz band. I was leading the band.

Yeah. With my band, I just, the way it happened that Oliver used to come around where we played at Lincoln Park and St. Catherine Hall and various places he was working. And so he said, why, why don't you give him a chance sometime? I said, well, when you get good enough. But I'm trying. I said, okay. So finally, Papa Mudd dropped out. You know, you had to do your day job or you couldn't do the job. And I told him, it was best for him to try to hold one job. If you want the other job, I'll have to get someone else or I'll take an Oliver. And how it happened that Oliver got in and got his name in the band. He had a friend named Gossoon. You know Gossoon? Gossoon is one of the best. Yeah. He's a good friend. So Joe called me up and said, have a couple of dates. Went out to the lake and went out to the economy hall. He said, Gossoon, I want to know, can you pay it for her? I said, sure I can pay it. I said, he knows the price? He said, yeah. So Gossoon put Oliver's name on his advertising machine and we started it. Before I was saying, get over if he's in King Oliver tonight. So he just volunteered and put Oliver's name with mine. Correct. So I didn't say no more about it.
Was Oliver about the same age as you or was he a little older?
Well, I think he was older. Joe was older.
Because Joe was too old for the number one war. Is that right? Joe Oliver, Bob Lyons, Lorenzo Stahl.
Well, or his drummer was very happy. He was too young.
My name was Oliver, myself, Oliver and Johnny Dash. Yeah.

Was you called in the next draft, I mean next call, I was supposed to go in the next one? I was called in the first one. They had me working in the shipyard in the morning. I was so happy. I said, everyone knock off, everything's okay. No more work. Boy, I jumped on top of the streetcar. Listen, you want me to talk? Yeah. You want me to talk? Yeah. You want me to talk?

Yeah. You want me to talk direct? Right. Huh? Yeah. I'm betting your remembrance background. Well, on a Monday night, we were playing at the Columny Hall. And, uh, Ori and Johnny Dash, they were looking for that paper, you know. They was worried about that paper. And I was the first one got the paper. I got the paper on a Monday morning. Well, at night, I went to the hall. And Johnny Dash was playing. And God soon didn't know what Johnny Dash was playing. Like a drunken fellow. I was worried. What's the light up there? What's the light up there? So, following Tuesday, you see, we would play for Mayor Boyman, back to Dixie Bury on
the band. Yeah. That's right.

Well, I was playing the band, not the, I'm not being in the band, but the Ori is. Well, they signed up, go to play the band. So, following Tuesday, I goes around to the Secretary of the Med, Mike Rooney. He said, oh, Mr. Mike. I said, I got there. He said, oh, don't worry about that. He says, they're gonna have your last recommendation. He says, you'll be better off over in Camp Pike. You'll go over there and you'll organize your band. I said, are there any other boys in the band? Married? I said, yeah. Well, I was single, me. I said, yeah. I said, I'm on the flat. He's been hired. He's kind of passing now. Well, tell the boys, go on back to their wives. Yeah. The guys was running wild, you know. They was running wild, you know. Neglecting home last summer. Remember?
Yeah.
Well, they made up with their wives.
I saved them. They saved them.
All right, I got those. I got those out there. Eight months. An awesome sign. I had eight furloughs.
That's pretty good, yeah. Went home every time.
Every month. Where was your station at that time?
A little rock, Camp Pike, I guess. I'd organized a tenth piece of orchestra. Called a receiving station jazz band.
You had a pretty soft.

And I, I had my trumpet out there, but my release was cornet. I had a Frank Holton cornet. And my violin. Well, when I got out there, they had a band of about three or four pieces that was organized. I'm speaking or you speaking?
That's all right, go ahead. Finish the story. Yeah. Anyway, ask Mr. Horace.

Well, after I got there, some recommendations, I had two of the boys from Bomb Bell Circus, two trumpet players. And of course they played circus style. We had a rehearsal. And I learned the fellas being out there in the camp at Georgia Boyd. I go and get Georgia, tell Lieutenant, I go and get Georgia Boyd. I got Walter Preston. You remember Walter Preston? He used to play banjo with Crisco? Yeah. Yes I do. Got him. And I went for Yank. Yank came around to the place. He goes for Lieutenant, Lieutenant Fleming from New York. He run the cabaret. He was a number one professional violinist. And he had a lot of brand new orchestration. Well, Yank comes. We had a little fella substituting there. He a fella, I tell you, remind me of Ori. His name was Willa Gaskin. He reminded me of Ori so much. He played trombone. But he was slow on it, you know. And of course, I was trying to get Yank in there. Because being from home, he's a Yank. And he walked off. Got cold feet. He went over to his company. So, I just had to make out with that boy. And I had on drums, a little boy used to be around Padre Street. He was a piano player. Called him Tommy Jackson. Now, maybe you're not remembering that. He was out there. He was drafted from Greenville. And he had a lot of ideas on drums. Well, I take him. And I went out from town and got a little polluted and got on the rock bar. Well, I had another boy in the camp in the first bathroom. Called him Baby Lovett.
He was from Alexandria.

So I take Baby in the band. I had my band. I had 10-piece archery. And I had to show him how we played. I'd take the trumpet and play Panama and all them numbers, you know. Just give them circus boys a swing. We got him down.
We worked pretty good. You never did have to go in the army then and then? Well, no.
Well, yeah.
Married.
We didn't meet up again.
I was married. But I was called for the next bachelor's booth to leave, you know.
Then it was too late to... Too late to...
That's the time I'd left him on top of the street, go. So crowded, you know. I had to get back home.

So when I came back to town, Joe had went to Chicago. Well, in 1917, Lewis was just playing three numbers. That's right. He played in the audience, he was a blues. He made a number called Wine and Grind. He named them. Sister Kate. Well, Sister Kate, take your finger out of Kattie's head. And then, of course, Joe Oliver and Jane Crying Swim, AJ P. Ron, take the number, went to New York and had it published as Sister Kate.
No, my mama's baby boy. Huh? I and my mama's baby boy. I've never seen the music. I've been trying to find it, but I can't find it in a place.
What, uh...
Sister Kate. Wasn't it Sister Kate? No.
Sister Kate was take your finger out of Kattie's head. Yeah. And they named it, If I Could Sheep Me Like My Sister Kate. Yeah. And C. Ron and Trance Williams.
That's right. They did publish that other thing with the...
But Wine and Grind was something about mama's... They named it different up there, I don't know what you call it.

Oh, I was wondering about Mutt. Was Mutt ever in the Army? Did he go in the Army, do you think? No, I don't think so. Oh, and I was interested before, when you said he was older than you, Mr. O'Reilly. Yeah. What was...
I think he missed, he just skipped it.
Yeah, I never did know his age. What was your birth date? If you don't mind giving it, then we'll have it straight on here.
My birthday? Christmas Day, December 25th. Born 1886. 1886. That's right.
Four o'clock in the morning.
Sure anymore. Sure anymore.
That was up in Laplace.
How do you pronounce that?
Well, Laplace. Laplace, that's what I say. And St. John's... St. John's parish. St. John's
St. John's Parish and the next parish is St. James Wilman Brodlip was born in St. James Parish
Did Pops Foster come from he came from Plaquemine
Plaquemine, Louisiana
I'm not sure He wasn't up in your neighborhood Pops Foster didn't come from that part of the country No
Well then Proceeding on
Yeah
I came back P. Lala Had opened up A kind of show On Claiborne Street

Remember that? Yeah. And Louis stepped up to play with the band. He had taken a list of the band and it was a cold night. On Sunday night I went there to see the band. Louis was up there and there was a straw hat on. It was freezing. That is mute. Who was that? Louis. Remember when Joe went away?
Well, I'd taken him with me or soon Joe left. He was working with me at Pete Lyle. Pete Lyle and I was running the place together.
That wasn't the place on the array. It was on the labor?
The labor ran between Conti and St. Louis. About near St. Louis. I hired Louis before Joe left.
That's what I'm saying. I come back, I find Louis.

Well, that's what he was playing with me. I left there and I started promoting dance at the economy hall and the co-op radio hall. Pete got mad because I didn't cut him in on my dance. He sent about 50 cops around there and they ran all my customers away.
I packed up and left. I came to Los Angeles. That's what happened to Jelly right here in this town.
San Francisco. What? The cops running customers away. Yeah.
They didn't do anything.
Just walk in and cement them. Yeah.
They just went out of the raid and that's that. That's what they went. Yeah. I was doing real fine too. Yeah. Because I was going to cut them in, you know.
Yeah. This place was too small. They couldn't hold enough people that I could make over nice work, you know.
For you in business you should make more than a salary, you know. Yeah.
You're promoting it. You're promoting it. You're going to hold all the expense and trouble. So then he wanted to cut in on me. I told him, no. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No.
No. No.
No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. He had the power, so you just don't go on down there and just write.
Well, I went back to the band. Joe was in the band. So we'd play, had cooperators around the corner, Sam Morgan.
Yeah.

Well, that's the place I promoted the interest to. He was in love with Larry Mack. And Joe asked to play from eight. Well in mind, it'd be alright if he could go make that little job from eight to eleven and put, he's called Lewis, he used to call him Dipper, put Dipper in his place. So, I said, you know, it's alright with me. Alright, you go play. So, here comes the Monday night. Opposition, Cooperative Hall and Comedy Hall. I had a little Joe at the theater. St. Louis. Yeah, we playing up there for God's soul. I go around there. They had a line up. That way and this way. Wouldn't go in the hall. Wouldn't go in the hall. We goes in and start a play. We players and players. Now the soul come in the hall. God's soul, he walked around. I said, why? I think he was playing regular enough, you know. Nobody come in the hall. I hung up a little money. Cooperative right on the corner there. People outside. Yeah, about eleven o'clock. Who come in his little foot there but Joe Oliver. When Joe Oliver come in the hall, it looked like a calf ass broke in. The whole hall packed right away. It wouldn't come in the hall. We played the same straight tunes. I leave, well I saw the boy was playing. I was leaving the band. It wasn't that over and over, over and over. Now no one had danced. Joe came in the hall, back up. All it was. So Joe got out, I said, Joe got out, I had been hugged with him. He was kicking that. He was kicking like that. Winter Garden was the same way. Remember the Winter Garden? That was the Winter Garden there.
Grabbing in my part.
That's right. Grabbing in my part. Over four backers.
You remember they raiding us? What? We just had a night to raid us.
Yeah, sure.
They were taking everyone to jail. Wasn't the same thing with Pete Lawley, you know. The guy running the roof guard, he got jealous of the place. Well it was.
Was that during Prohibition already? What they raided for?
No.
Prohibition was on then.

Yeah. Prohibition was on then. And so they came in, the place was packing jammed. They just loaded the wagon up, just going after that. And we sat in the front of the bandstand. And we said, oh well, we all right. And one of the big cops looked up there and said, how about the band, Sergeant? And I said, I'm in.
Well, I paid two and a half. And really break up the competition.

And that's the night Joe, I told him, he said, I'm going to leave here. I had an offer to go to Chicago. He had a telegram. I said, you want to leave town? He said, I said, yeah. Right this guy. I said, I don't want to go. All right now. And Joe was taking the job and he had Jimmy to go with him. And I went station with them and it was broke, the Ten Commandments. And I said, how you boys sick for your lunch on the train? They haven't gotten any money. So I gave him $10 each, Jimmy and Joe.
Was that Jimmy Noon?

Yeah. He was playing with me at the time, Joe. I got a telegram. And right after it was ready, Joe made up his mind to leave. And I had a telegram. I didn't want to go. So I turned the job over to Joe. And he's taking Jimmy with him.

Now, I'm going to proceed on with you now. Me and him was buddies. You know. We'd go out on Mondays, you know, and of course, Kid Ore. He's a drawing card. He said Kid Ore is everything because we had all the work. I got on my office and I'm going to leave this town. I got to go to California. I got to go. Remember when I came over and talked to my mom? Yes. I got to come over to my house on a Monday and talk to my mother. Come over there about ten o'clock in the morning. Monday morning and talk. You know, you could talk French, you know. My mother was sometime well up and down, and when she meet her point she could speak French like that, you know, talk, talk, talk. I said, you think that's my house that day?
Yeah.

So in the evening comes her. You have a good memory. She, let me tell you, I'm not even finished talking. So she come in the back, we had a dinner, we dressed. She said, oh he's a nice boy. She said, he's a nice boy. She said, I told him, you could go, but when I get sick, you come home. Boy told him, yeah, if you get sick I come home. Alright, we dressed, we come over. He said, well, I left my boy with Gus, who's going to take? He said, well, I say, Dipper, Johnny Dots. I see Joe Oliver, he had a preference of drumming, and Ori had a preference of drumming. Ori liked it, Joe Lindsey, and Joe Lindsey was crazy for him. And Joe Oliver, he liked that little red happy. Well, Ori leave him, take red happy. He was Oliver's drummer then.
Well, Joe wasn't anxious to work then from the moment he wanted to be a gambler, you know. He ran 25 or so.
But you liked his time.
Yeah. He liked his drum time. Much easier to get along with, too.

I said, well, alright, now, now we got together. Ori gets together. Ori, get the boys together. If the horse going, oh, the floor is going. Horse, I'll go. Horse going. Ori, we get to the place, listen at this now. Ben Mulligan's had the saloon grabbing in that part. In the back, at a supper. And it was prohibition during that time, but Ben Mulligan, a big politician in the parish prison right around the corner, next block. Ben had liquor there that's like, nah. He had anything he wanted. But only that time, he was loud as hell, and Virginia there, and a little beer. That's all for me.
Sweet Lucy.

Yeah. So, Ori put, they had a supper, and long table, and waitin', little piggy around there. Nah, they had to sway in. They all got all that mean to the sport. Johnny Topp, and Lewis, and Joe Lindsey. You want to see, I said, listen. I said, I didn't tell them I was going to promise them. My mother. You going? I said, yeah, I'm going. I tell you, stop going. All right. Ori left on a Friday night. They went by the train. I couldn't make it that Friday night to see you all. Ori goes out, comes out to Los Angeles, and he meets up with a dude, he called Lee Lockin. From Galveston, Texas. Right. He called the fella, he had plenty of money, was out there lookin' for a place to open. And there was an old Cadillac that had been closed, at 5th or Central, right across the depot during that time. They got together, and we didn't do it. I'm going to say something now. You know, when Ori was in town, in Los Angeles, well, they had a lot of people from the Orioles, kid Ori was in town. Gee. And men had enough advertising. They'd tell each other, oh. Well, we went out before things were straight. I mean, the sport was sprees, you know. Well, that's why I wasn't there then, but it was told to be. And they had this black band that had been playing in the Dreamland. That time, that time, they'd tell me they was playing there about 27 years old. Yeah.
Not long ago.

Yeah. So, Ori, one Sunday night they gets him in there, a little high or something. They got him on the stand, and I don't know what they tell me. They're throwing the vamp on the Orioles, you know. And, uh, tell them you plop down there, you know, vamp, and pick up, you know. I don't have a thing now.
No, they just knocked you off there. They didn't even know how to say what they were going to play.
Didn't give you a chance to get him there at all. No. Well, that's right.

So, finally, they came right back with Tiger Rag, you know. They tried to trick you on that first. Mm-hmm. And boy, then I knew they was going to play, and they were playing in the right key, you know, the ring. And that was it.

So, uh, one day, I got out there then. Now, how it was, Frank Doosan had been out here, and they sent him back by not reading. And he said, here, he done sent the tickets to me on Lewis Armstrong, Johnny Dots, and Joe Lindsey. He's expecting. Of course, today, some fellas don't know that until today. I'm sure that happened now. I was going to get out. So, I had a ticket. I goes to Johnny Dots' house. Johnny Dots and his wife will accept me in. How to find him on a call. He had told his wife about it, but he had saw the porters at that porters inn on Rampart Street where the porters come in and bum, you know. Johnny Dots, they went to the porters and told the porters, well, he's going to leave, we're going to California. He said, who's going to California? He said, me, and all of them, and all of them. He said, what do you tell you, Johnny? He said, you better stay here because you're going to go out there and they're going to send you right back like they've done Frank Doosan. So, what Johnny does, he goes to work and see Lewis. At Patina Sartoga Lewis was living right there. He said, what do you tell me?

next to the ballroom. He goes with him and let's have a conversation over there. I don't know. I goes to his house. He didn't tell me. I noticed coming in a car, Louisiana Avenue car coming down. Now we come from Uptown to come see Dipper, get off at Petita and Rampart. I noticed he was kind of funny. He wouldn't say nothing. I said, well, he said, no, he wouldn't say nothing. So I said, well, I guess Dipper Rampart gets off. He goes down there, there's a little up in the place there, that ballroom there, a fella sitting on a bill box playing piano, a fella with a drum and lay at us, call it there. You know how he'd go for that. I can't go right. Yes, Mr. Hoss. Yes, Mr. Hoss. I said, oh, no, come outside. We talk about the wine. No wine.

Like when you mentioned that, you know, things were getting too hot in New Orleans, so to speak, the cops breaking stuff up and everything. What was the attraction in California? I mean, why did California come to your mind rather than some other place outside New Orleans?
Well, Joe.
Is that in San Francisco as well as the West Coast or was it just L.A.?

No, first I was supposed to meet Joe in Chicago and join him, you know. Yeah. They'll get back together. And I heard about this good climate out here, you see. And I changed my mind and I came to Los Angeles. And when I was here, Joe, I told him I didn't know whether I was going to stay or not, so he wired me ticket to stay in the office a whole month. But then still I didn't make up my mind. And by the time I made up my mind that I wasn't going to Chicago, I sent, I wrote the manual and I asked manual one editor to get the boys together just as he finished telling you. And Lee Locken wanted me to work for him. So we closed the black and tan down just about, couldn't get enough people to pay the expense. Somehow, then I left and all the boys went back home and I opened mud and Wade Whaley, wasn't it? Well, no. Yeah, you went home. I'll explain it to you if you want. No, you're a little wrong. You left after the Cadillac clothes.

I'll tell you how it was. No, let me tell you how it was. I'll foreseeing and tell you how it was. Yes, go ahead. Well, after they backed out, I went out. I had the tickets in my pocket. My brothers, I'm so worried. I'm going to say, well, wait a while. I said, I promised to go out with the boy and I got the tickets. She said, well, wait a while. I'll wait a while. Well, on a Sunday morning, about 4 o'clock, 4.30 in the morning, who comes to my house, 3.31 L. Street, damn. Knocked me out that night. But Walter Deku. Walter Deku come to my house, chills and fever. Knocked on the door and my mother went to the door and offered him inside. So it was pretty sick and she said, oh, just tell me to come to the door. She said, come tell me. I'll go to the door and I said, look, oh, she said.
She won't bother anything. She won't bother anything. Let her play. I won't hurt anything.

Okay. All right. Go ahead now. So I says, all right, he's do favors for me. So I goes out to the bungalow at West End. And who they had out there, Walter Deku, well, I was playing this place a week. I take the job a week this place. Who they had out there but Mud Carey, Wade Whaley, and a little fella called Mack Hill stuck a bone on his feet. He died. The drum out there. Look at us out there. And I went there. So glad I came along because Wade used to buy music all the time and Walter Deku didn't read and he just played like he wanted. People liked it and he played that for years. Well, I never had nobody.

Well, I won it. And they throw it back to Sacramento, you see. Oh, yeah. And with a license of that kind, you can't, after 30 days, it's cancer. You can't use it, see. So it went back and it hit to the right because we couldn't get ready. You're all set to open the new place now. Yeah, he told me, go ahead. Well, I get it or not. We have the number, you know.
Yeah. Well, I was going to ask a minute ago about Joe Lindsey. Was he really such a good drummer? He never played in late years, you know, and so he gave up music.

Yeah, much time. No, very good. He really liked him, huh? The best time keeping drummer I ever had, ever played, was with Hendrick Martin. Yeah, he'd been to your drummer for years. Oh boy. Guy had an idea. Any number you'd play with, any little funny lyrics to it or something, that would mean a bird or a rabbit or a rat, anything, he'd get some kind of instrument to imitate it, you know. A little track. Yeah, fill in, you know. Like a cow, you know. Good coloration. Yeah. Oh yeah, a big bag full of that stuff. That's true. So you want me to keep on that?
Well, just one second. I was going to ask, I'll finish up to the Henry Martin business. How come he wasn't with you? Did he live long or was he dead by that time?
He was working in Storoville quite a while with Manuel Perez. He worked with me when, you know, he was on there one night, you see.
Yeah, I wonder why you didn't want to take him to California too.

No, he had quit playing. He was playing guitar when I left there. Oh really? Then he went back to the drum. I was so old and he couldn't make it. He just got away from it. Go ahead, Nancy. Nah, go ahead. Thanks.

So, alright. We started playing that night, playing all them numbers and you know Wade had a habit when he was talking. Y'all used to call him Busher. So, alright. He said, you know something? Man, if I had a lineup like this, go to California, Cali. Cali, we clean up. I said, let me tell you, a white band right around the corner of my house. He was begging for a band. I'm there. Oh man. I said, leave any time. Yeah? Now I'm playing at Walter's Place. Alright. Got together. Pop a mug, pop a mug, pop a mug, roll a mug. Well, he could spell. Wade could be nice. Alright. Guess Alfred Williams? After little Mac Hill was playing out there, stuck a gun. He was on his feet and died. They go and get Mac, they ask me who did I like. I told them, well Alfred Williams kept a good time. He was Sam Morgan, so they go down. I said, now listen, how you gonna do this boy's band, this boy kid now? I said, I'm just playing here this father and son in my last week with this boy. Wade said, I'll get old man George McCullen to go out and play all but his piano player. Walter's coming back on the job. Alright. So everything's alright. One or two they'll say, let's pee, where's the runner? They was fixing the road. We went over on a teepee. Made us a little late. So, I wouldn't say nothing to them boys, mucking them. Nothing. About Lewis and all them got cold feet. They don't know what they were going to do. So, there we go. They get out there when the train, get to California. What I done, I grab my grip and get ahead of them dudes you know. Where horse at? Where horse? They was way behind me. Where horse? I want to get off first so I can see or it expand, alright. So yeah, I get off, yeah, they were way behind me. When they get off, they're out there and they're out there. They're all ready. He's locked. I'm looking down. I can see, I can see, alright. I say, alright. I don't say nothing until I speak to you. I said, alright. Or else, ain't that Papa Mark? I said, yeah. He's looking at you. He's seeing a little black fella coming. Ain't that Boucher? I said, yeah. I see that little fella coming. Ain't that average? So, we're right across from the Cadillac. So, I said, won't send him to the Cadillac. Well, Lord, got, ooh, of course. We got on the dress roll, and I said, you know something? He said, God, sir, it's good. He said that them men did come. So, we started playing. Now, all the shows with the man. Ha-ha. We done in Yardins. Make an advertisement. Which houses out in California at that time? You see a two-story house with gyres on them? Them dudes was blocked in with a block. They never sat on their porch upstairs. They had an old guy out here who was waiting for the lockers. They called him Chappy Henderson. Master Ceremony. So, Ory explained, get a truck. We used to get, we used to have two mules pulling the furniture wagon when we'd advertise. Ory explained, go hark in the truck, all right? One got a big old truck back on the truck. Put the piano in the truck. Chappy says, I'll know, I'll work to him just to go on in good spots, you know. All right. I went to Manor, big old house there, and blockhead it. People never been one of that guy since he's been out there. He's born ripped, Chappy Henderson. And, oh, we got one in the corner, the striker, brown skin, who you for? And then people upstairs, come on, bust the door down. I never heard any music like that. Well, that's all right. We made it out of time. What part of town was that? In Los Angeles. What part of town was it? Right across the city, that point, 5th to Central. We didn't get to Hollywood, but the
news got out there, you know. And all the movies started, you know. So, we made it out of time.
You know that night? That's where the money was, you know. All that night, Mr. Jack?
But in fact, we planted money there and away with everyone. The place was packed like sardines.

The Dreamland right around the corner. Big store called Billings, Dreamland. We played, packed like sardines. We played, played. Money come on a Saturday night, they raid the place. They put everybody in jail, but they look at the band. They want to put us in jail, but the champions say, oh no, we didn't party. They didn't lock you up that time then? No. All right. Well, that was really bad, didn't they? That was going out of the field then. Going out of the field. All right. Well, got in the field. Well, they sent back for them. Got his permit back, my brother, and one or so. We started again. Started playing again. All right. They raid again. That was all. I said, well. Now they was in the field then, because we was playing, jobs, we took that big red truck, whether the bullfight and all that. Get together, gigging jobs. So, I got a telegram from my mother. My mother was very sick. Yeah, at the Coliseum, you know. Very sick. Well, the Coliseum. Yeah. I go to the, I go to the depot. Here come a train running from Los, from Frisco to Los Angeles. A fellow pulled on there, his name was Poissy Wright. Poissy Wright from New Orleans.

He just died about a month ago, Ed Garland told us. Poissy Wright died? Wasn't it? Wasn't he the one? I don't know where he is. No, that was the bouncer. The bouncer died. Who was the big chaper? Oh, you're talking about Zach Williams. Zach Williams died about a month ago.

Flo Walker. Big Zach. Yeah. He used to be a, used to wake and move it, yeah. He bought my memories up together now. Well, all right. Poissy, what are you doing coming out the depot? I said, I'm just coming over and looking at the race. He says, well, what's the trouble? I said, well, I'll show him a telegram. He said, oh, I'm sorry. I live on San Pedro Street. He said, I'll tell you what I'm doing. I'm going, we're going to make a trip all the way to El Paso tonight at 1130. And when you get over there, I connect you with Big George Jones running from the Orleansdale Passer and said, he'll ride you down home. It's all right. When I goes back home, the telephone rang. Then I got home. Telephone, who it was, but Overy, and the boss of the Dreamland came to sign a contract. And I told you all I couldn't. You remember the little girl used to come sit up and play sometime? I'd even play the piano. Yeah. I can't recall her name. So you all hired her, didn't I? Yeah. And, uh, Selma. Selma, Selma. Selma, I don't know. I don't know her name.
I don't know her name. That's skinny girl. Yeah. That's a much wife. Huh? Is that much married? Or a different girl? No.
Tell me, much married. He told me married a girl who used to play. Oh, you used to talk about Madeline. Mm-hmm.
Was she the one who played? Yeah. Yeah, it was Madeline, but the other girls played some too. Yeah, I love it. But these little girls come out and play good. Madeline.
The one with, he told me, married. Yeah, that's right. Yeah, we thought about it. So, uh.
I'll go and test them out. That's all right. Let's be starting a visit. Don't worry about it.

So, after grand opening that night, so what I does, Poison says, I go to the airport and meet him at seven o'clock. He says, well we got a lot of time. I says, let's go around. I say, your band is open for the Dream Line. I say, yeah. I say, let's go around. We went around and there's a packing jam. I think on Big Zack Show, the Bremier of the Bandstand. It was so packed. He was sticking with us. He said, get out the way. They all get out the way. He said, just say, please. Same band, we left with him just like there was a little band. So I plays there with him until about eleven o'clock. He didn't leave eleven o'clock. And I plays there with him in the girls' place. Remember that? And I left. I left for him, went home. I saw him, I hadn't saw him no more until I came out here at the hanging room about four
years ago. What year was that? Four years was the hanging room.
You mean when you were first out here?
Uh, nineteen, nineteen.
Well, it was nineteen, nineteen when we was out here.
Every time when we left, when he left, it was twenty then.
Well, I stayed out here. It was only four months when my mother got saved.
Well, that rag you used to play in nineteen, nineteen, is that named after those days? Or what was that rag?
Well, it was an old march we used to play, you know. We didn't know the title of it, you know. Yeah. No one had music. And the brass band used to play, you know.
Well, there was no brass band march.
So Louie and I got together and we got to play in this, you know. And we just called it nineteen, nineteen.
Yeah.

Louie told Harry Sutton one day, we stand by the corner. After all that went around there and played. Me, Mutt and Laurie stand by the pool room. And we come along with Harry Sutton. Oh boy. The old boy said, a hammer wasn't big enough to cut my head. He had to get an act to chop my head off. So I saw that. He walked up. He said, I know. He had told Lee, well Lee, Lee Larkin, well he used to go around his barber shop and squint and he went around and went around. He told Lee, he said, well Lee says, all the band is like Aura, say you say, throwin' your money away. And he said that. Who said that? Huh? That's what Harry Sutton had told Lee. So, and Lee comes tell Aura that. Yeah. So when Aura Sutton was telling the corner of David, Aura told his face, that thing that walked off with a body. He said nothing.
When did you go to Chicago, how long did you stay out of Chicago? How long did you stay out here then?
Did you join Oliver right away? Did you join Kid Oliver when you went to Chicago again?

No, I worked with Louie. Louie left for, Louie wrote my letter too, told me he's coming down, Lee Plutcher and he's coming to Chicago to record. He heard I was going to be in Chicago. He would like to have him record with him at the Hot Five, you know. So I recorded with Louie and Louie got the job at the Dream. So we were drawing so well and Louie asked for more money, you know. And the guy in bottom, owner, he refused to pay him more money. So Louie said, well, let's not work. I said, okay. He said, I got the job at the Dream. I said, well, I'll go with Oliver. But still, we still record. And I recorded with eight bands for five years, regular. I recorded so many numbers, I hadn't even heard them. Different bands. I would have recorded more, but I couldn't take it.
Oh yeah.

And before that I got a job after the Dream and the Clos, working from eight to, I'm sorry, eight to twelve at Municipal Pier in Chicago. I went to Tate's Big Band. Oh, Thurston Tate. Yeah. And I worked until twelve o'clock in Dutray, taking sick. I'm a little ahead of my story then. And I went to the entertainers and worked with Carl Dixon from one to five. And after Dutray got well, then I went with Oliver. That's where it was.
Where was the entertainers? On 35th? Yeah, 35th.
Same place at Plantation and... Long in Mexico.
What was their name?

Joe Glavie. Sunset. Sunset. And then Ness was across the street, yeah. So they wanted me to get a band, a recording band together. But I had to sign a contract. I was freelancing. I recorded with all the bands. You see? When you first recorded in Los Angeles?
Yeah.
Yeah, I made much of $600 one day. In Chicago? Yeah. When we were talking...
We were talking with two bands.

Ma Rainey came there with a call, a call over the blues singer, you know. Some could sing, some couldn't. And all the bands got tired. But Lil and I, myself... And you kept going. They'd leave and go send a call up a trumpet player or a clarinet player, Johnny Dyson play. They all burned out. I stood there and made the money.
Did you record with Ma Rainey once? There was a rumor that you'd made, actually made records with Ma Rainey yourself.
Not my band, but I record with the group.
You did?
Yeah.
Back of Ma Rainey.
Yeah, that's right. I've never heard the records.
Down in Los Angeles, we were talking about those Nardscog records. They say he's still living and still has that same old recording machine that you made your first records on.
Yeah.
Can you remember about who had that date? Was that the Spikes Brothers?
Spikes Brothers. Those are the ones Manuel was telling you about had a dreamland, you know. Yeah. We went to work for us. We left the other place and shift around. They were musicians too, you know.
But they were promoters too. They had the dreamland. Yeah. They ran the dreamland.

Yeah. They bought it from some other guy after we went, what is the place where we played? Cadillac. Cadillac. The guy sold it to Spikes Brothers and we went back and went for Spikes Brothers. Manly come down and started us off and he left. Oh, my mother was there. Yeah. Well, you stayed, you couldn't stay.
Yeah. Well, were they connected with the Spikes Brothers circus at all? Those Spikes Brothers? No. Different people out there.
And they had a record shop and music, you know, 12th and Central there.
Did you ever play with Jelly Roll out here on the coast in California? No. Did you ever work with Jelly?
No. I only recorded with Jelly in Chicago.
Did you ever play any other dates with Jelly or just the records?
Just records. Just the records. Jelly never had a band. In Chicago he'd go around all the clubs and pick the men he wanted for recording. Yeah. Any records. Any records.
Didn't they have any recording facilities at all in New Orleans? No. And then at that time no one in New Orleans was recording? No.
First time I saw a recording outfit and when I recorded for Spike Brothers, Ross Andres.
It was Fred Washington, is the pianist, was he on that date?
Yeah, that's right.
Fred Washington.
Dink Johnson. Yeah. Dink Pat his feet so loud, we got a pillar, and then we stood up on a pillar, and the pillar wouldn't do so we got a mattress.
Dink. Dink.
Yeah. He'd never go to bed if he wasn't playing. That's all right.
Did you just record two parts, two numbers? It was four.
Oris Creole Trauma, Crooked Blues, and two more because they had two girls singing, they both sang.
Oh yeah, that's right. Yeah. Two singers. I can't remember that.
I have the record here someplace.
Yeah. Well that's your little girl, have her to say your name, right? What's your name?
Tell me your name. Tell me your name. Tell me your name. Tell me your name. Tell me your name.
What's your name? Say Bruce.
Wait. Tell me. Tell me that. That's Mike. Come on. We call her Bruce for short, but her name is Babette. What is your name? She's a little girl. She's no... Sir Dice, huh? She no address. She does.
That's all right. That's all right.
She's no dice. We've got a dice game on.
I never thought we could pick them up then. Why was William? Well we were talking about those records and that, you made of the Spikes Brothers and Dink
and all. Dink died, you know, a couple years ago.
Yes. About four years, I guess. Yeah.
And the records went up to $90 a piece.

Dr. Extra paid $90 for his income. Yeah, those are hard to find. And when they started going up, I heard about it. It was selling for $35 and kept going up. So I went to Spikes. And then I went to Spikes. And then I went to Spikes. And then I went to Spikes. And then I went to Spikes.

And then I went to Spikes Brothers and Dink and all. And then I went to Spikes Brothers and Dink and all. Dink died, you know, a couple years ago. Yes. About four years, I guess. Yeah, I heard. And the record went up to $90 a piece. Dr. Extra paid $90 for his income.
Yeah, those are hard to find.

And when it started going up, I heard about it. It was selling for $35 and kept going up. So I went to Spikes, Rip Spikes. And I said, Rip, what happened to the master record, the Sunshine Label? I recorded it. You want to sell them? I haven't got them. He said, well, we sold the house and we left them in the garage and the people threw them in the alley. And then when I told him what happened, how the record was selling, you know, what people were getting for them, boy, he didn't know what to say. But I wasn't going to tell them until I buy them from him and get a receipt, you know.
It didn't work, though.
No, it didn't work.
But the Spike brothers all dead now? Both brothers dead? I know.
I know. I saw where Johnny died, the piano player. I think Rip is still living here around Los Angeles. And where it...
Yeah, Rip had a band that recorded later for Columbia, didn't he? Was that his own band, Bill? Rip Spikes?
Yeah. Rip Spikes? Uh-huh.
Yeah. In Los Angeles?
I don't know where.
Must have been. Must have been. He's never seen one record about 1927 or so.
Well, he's been there. Could have been Los Angeles. Yeah.
There was a Columbia recording. Uh-huh. Well, I asked you the other night on the phone about Wade Whaley. You think he's in San Diego. Do you? Where did you see him last?
Last time I saw him there, in 45, I was working at the Jade Room. My client had to go to Seattle, Joe, Dennisburg, you know?
Yeah.
And he had some business center, so I'd wait for a few nights, you know?
Yeah.

And he was living in a project there in Watts. And I went there and I said, we used to go to work. He was working days, you know? And uh, his wife said, if you do work, you have to keep it quiet because you have a job in the shipyard or something. I said, what difference does that make? I said, uh, you can do ten jobs as long as you do his work on the other job, you know? Yeah. So he's got to be a henpeck, you know? Yeah. And uh, he played until Joe came back and I haven't seen him since. No.
We haven't been able to hear anything about him. Nobody knows where he is. No.
No.
Your girl's calling. She's out there. Girl's calling. She's on there. Have you ever heard that he was around San Jose? Who? Wait, wait, wait, wait.
He wasn't San Jose before he moved down there. Before then. Because his banjo, the secretary of the union here used to play banjo with him. He died about two years ago. Forbes. Yeah, Forbes.
I asked him about him.
He said he didn't know where he was located. I don't know if he's dead or what.
Gee, is it two years since Forbes died? Huh? It doesn't seem like two years since Forbes died. No, I didn't say two years.
I said...
Well, you talked to him two years ago about it. About it, yeah.
Yeah. I was in Los Angeles when he thought about it. That's just by a little over a year.
Yeah, I was thinking about a year.
I was at Beverly Cavern then when he died. He died during the strike. The cemetery strike? Yeah.
Yeah, that's right, yeah.

They couldn't bury him for a long time. He stayed on ice, you know. You like it in Northern California now better than Los Angeles? Yeah. I do. I'm in account of the smog, you know. Uh-huh. And it's more of a city to me. San Francisco in my sense. It's more like New York, but still I like it better than I do New York. But mostly the smog I hate down there. I thought I was going to have scientists, you know. Oh, yeah. I hate it with this stuff. We love smoke and dust. That's why I'm going down to play like that. Those guys at Beverly Cavern, I want them to stay as long as I want. The 4400 Club Theater. So I feel better here. Yeah, that's good.
You like it over on this?
Especially when we were living here now, you know, the climate is so good. And rest good. And rest good. And no worry.
You haven't been back to New Orleans except just to go through there.
Yeah, I went through that on my way to Europe and back. stuff like stuff
But I only spent a few hours there, I told you, when I went down the foyer on my way to Europe and I ran a call, my wife and I, went out the lake, going to eat some nice seafood, you know.
You still have a sister living, a sister lives up in Laplace?
No, she died. Oh, she's... She died about four years ago, live over four years.
And Johnny fought me.
And I have a sister involved in one in Los Angeles.
Oh yeah. And Johnny?
Johnny died. Out here? Los Angeles. He and I had chicken for him, you know.
Yeah, I heard Johnny but I didn't know where it was.
And what I was doing when Austin Weld asked me to come play with, you know, on the show. My brother died in 39.
That's when I first met you there.
Yeah.
Remember when I went to see you, the first time you had a saxophone in your hand, you'd been arranging something. Yeah.
I still have it. You still use it? I only had saxophone, clarinet, trumpet and... and carnet, bass, valve trombone, I had a song like that.
Did you ever play valve trombone before you took up the slide or...
That was my first.
Your first instance.
I played trumpet too, you know. What was your very... You know, if you'd say a couple of weeks I'd be perfect on it. Yeah. I used to sing the same with the valve. Yeah.
True. What was your very first instrument?
A homemade banjo. Homemade banjo.
I made myself.

I made five instruments. Banjo, mandolin, bass, violin, guitar and a lead violin. I used to sing them up with fishing cards and... and different kind of wire we would get. And we sang along with it and fish riding.
Yeah.
Out in the class.
How old were you when you moved to New Orleans? I was always wondering...
Oh, I was 21. I had to stay there until I was 21. But I used to visit them all then.
Used to visit. But you waited for about 21 to move down. Yeah.

And when I bought my first goods out from Baltimore... paid $65 that I was blowing at my sister's house. And the bull didn't happen to be passing on the sidewalk and he heard it. And I'm going to go and say... Oh, you the young man blowing that horn? Yeah. And the young man trying to blow it. He said, well, you sound good. He said, I'm the king.
I said, King who is there? King Baldwin. Oh, I said, how are you, Mr. Baldwin, King?

He said, would you like to play with me? I said, very much so. I said, wait a minute. I ran back in the kitchen in the sister's back. I said, oh, that one made a wife. And boy, I was so happy. He said, no, you have to go back home and go to school. You promised your dad he was on the staff there in the 21. And when it was 21, 4 o'clock in the morning and 8 o'clock I was on the train. I've been gone ever since. Well, I was playing professionally, playing dances, you know. Oh, yeah, sure. That was about 18 then. About 18-4 then, huh? Yeah. And when it was 21, 4 o'clock in the morning, and 8 o'clock I was on the train. I've been gone ever since.
How old were you, Ren Bold, and heard you?
Well, I was about 18 then. Well, I was playing professionally, playing dances, you know.
Oh, yeah, sure. That was about 18-4 then, huh?

Yeah. I had me an old valve trombone, you know. And I had some in the holes, and I used to put soap in it. I had $4 a week. And as long as the soap didn't get damp, you know, I was going. I was all right. You get damp, you don't want bubbles. Bubbles, yeah. Told the guys, go ahead, I'll catch up where I put some more soap. Yeah, I was the first guy of a blue bubble. It was pretty tough, but we had lots of fun.
And those were the days.
Not much money, but lots of fun, wasn't it, huh? Oh, yeah. I wasn't worried about money. You wake up broke, whistling, and just happy. Now, if you wake up broke, boy, you want to cry. 된 stuff

segments.title: Mic check and Ory and Manetta's reunion
segments.summary: Setting up the microphone; Ory and Manetta greet each other after about four years, and Manetta mentions his blood pressure.

segments.title: First time Ory and Manetta played together
segments.summary: They recall playing first at Tom Anderson's and later at Storyville, with Ory's move to Los Angeles in 1919 as the next time.

segments.title: How Joe Oliver's name got into Ory's band
segments.summary: Ory explains how Oliver, after Papa Mutt dropped out, got the job and his name was put on the advertising with Ory's band.

segments.title: The draft call and Manetta's band-leader exemption
segments.summary: Draft ages, Ory's shipyard job, and Manetta's story of getting his call-up and being told to organize a band at Camp Pike.

segments.title: Manetta's receiving-station jazz band at Camp Pike
segments.summary: Manetta organizes a ten-piece jazz band, recruiting players including Baby Lovett, and Ory explains why he was not drafted.

segments.title: Louis's blues and the song Sister Kate
segments.summary: Manetta recalls Louis in 1917 and the numbers Wine and Grind and Sister Kate, and how they were published elsewhere under other names.

segments.title: Ory's birth date and Laplace origins
segments.summary: Asked about Oliver's age, Ory gives his birth date (Dec 25, 1886), his birthplace in St. John Parish, and talk of Pops Foster's origin.

segments.title: Louis takes over at Pete Lala's
segments.summary: Manetta returns to find Louis in the band at Pete Lala's; Ory says he hired Louis before Oliver left.

segments.title: Ory promotes his own dances and Pete Lala has the police stop them
segments.summary: Ory leaves Pete Lala's to promote dances, Pete wants a cut, and sends cops to chase off his customers.

segments.title: Joe Oliver draws the crowd at the cooperative hall; police raids
segments.summary: Manetta describes a Monday night when no one entered until Oliver arrived, then raids on the dance halls during Prohibition.

segments.title: Oliver leaves for Chicago with Jimmy Noone
segments.summary: Ory turns the job over to Oliver, who takes a Chicago telegram offer and Jimmy Noone, and Ory gives them train money.

segments.title: Manetta tells his mother he is going to California
segments.summary: Manetta recounts getting his mother's permission, the drummer preferences of Ory and Oliver, and the farewell supper.

segments.title: Ory's first night at the Los Angeles Cadillac
segments.summary: Ory in Los Angeles with Lee Lockin, and a rival band trying to trick him on a Sunday night until Tiger Rag.

segments.title: Johnny Dodds and the others get cold feet
segments.summary: Manetta had train tickets for Louis, Johnny Dodds and Joe Lindsey, but they backed out after the porters warned them.

segments.title: Why Ory chose California over Chicago
segments.summary: Ory says he was meant to join Oliver in Chicago but heard of the good climate and stayed in Los Angeles.

segments.title: Manetta takes the West End job with Wade Whaley and Mutt Carey
segments.summary: Walter Decou fetches Manetta to a bungalow job in West End, with Mutt Carey and Wade Whaley, while Ory explains a licence delay.

segments.title: Joe Lindsey and Henry Martin as drummers
segments.summary: Ory praises Henry Martin's timekeeping and sound effects, and explains why he was not brought to California.

segments.title: Manetta travels to Los Angeles and the Cadillac opens
segments.summary: The train trip west, the advertising truck, the packed Cadillac at 5th and Central, and a packed house.

segments.title: Raids at the Cadillac and Manetta called home to New Orleans
segments.summary: The Cadillac is raided, Manetta gets a telegram about his mother and meets Poissy Wright, and the Dreamland offers a contract.

segments.title: Manetta plays the Dreamland with Zack Williams and goes home
segments.summary: Playing at the packed Dreamland, then going home; Ory and Manetta settle that they were in Los Angeles in 1919-20.

segments.title: The tune 1919 and Harry Sutton's remark about Ory
segments.summary: Ory explains that 1919 was an old march Louis and he named, and Manetta tells a story about Harry Sutton and Lee Lockin.

segments.title: Ory goes to Chicago, records with Louis and joins Oliver
segments.summary: Ory leaves in 1925, records with Louis's Hot Five, then plays with Oliver, Tate and Carl Dixon at Chicago jobs.

segments.title: Chicago clubs and freelance recording pay
segments.summary: The Entertainers on 35th, Ory's refusal to sign an exclusive contract, and earning up to $600 in a day freelancing.

segments.title: Ma Rainey calls and Ory's work behind her
segments.summary: Ory describes outlasting other players at a Ma Rainey session and confirms he recorded behind her.

segments.title: The Spikes Brothers, the Dreamland and the first records
segments.summary: The Spikes Brothers bought the Dreamland and ran a record shop; Ory recalls the first recording equipment he saw.

segments.title: Working and recording with Jelly Roll Morton
segments.summary: Ory recorded with Jelly Roll in Chicago only, and notes New Orleans had no recording at the time.

segments.title: The Spikes Brothers Sunshine session with Dink Johnson
segments.summary: Ory recalls Fred Washington and Dink Johnson, padding for Dink's foot tapping, and the four sides including Ory's Creole Trombone.

segments.title: Interruption with the child during the recording
segments.summary: A little girl comes in and the interviewer and Ory talk to her before resuming.

segments.title: The rare Sunshine records and Rip Spikes
segments.summary: The records now sell for $90; Ory tells how Rip Spikes lost the masters, and they discuss the brothers' later fates.

segments.title: Searching for Wade Whaley
segments.summary: Ory last saw Wade Whaley in 1945 in Watts; the interviewer asks if he might be in San Diego or San Jose.

segments.title: Ory prefers Northern California; visit to New Orleans
segments.summary: Ory prefers the Bay Area to smoggy Los Angeles and says he only stopped for hours in New Orleans on his way to Europe.

segments.title: Ory's sisters and brother
segments.summary: The deaths of Ory's sister in Laplace and his brother Johnny in Los Angeles.

segments.title: Ory's instruments and his homemade first banjo
segments.summary: Ory lists the instruments he plays, says valve trombone was first, and describes building homemade instruments.

segments.title: Meeting King Baldwin and moving to New Orleans at 21
segments.summary: Ory stays in Laplace until 21, is heard by a bandleader who invites him to play, and leaves the morning he turns 21.

segments.title: Early professional days with a valve trombone and soap
segments.summary: Ory recalls patching his valve trombone with soap, earning $4 a week, and being happy despite poverty.
